notes: Food for home consumption is exempt.

Drinks served by mixed-beverage permit holders (bars and restaurants) pay the 8.25% mixed beverage sales tax instead of the general sales tax, and the permit holder pays a 6.7% mixed beverage gross receipts tax on the same sales: 14.95% of the drink price, counted here. Cities and counties get a share of these taxes rather than levying their own. Beer and wine served by a mixed-beverage permit holder pay both taxes too; restaurants with only a wine and malt beverage permit collect the regular sales tax (6.25% plus local) instead, which isn't separated here: no official figure gives their share of drinks served.
Household supplies: diapers, baby wipes and baby bottles are exempt (since September 1, 2023), which is not taken out here.
Personal care products: menstrual and postpartum products, breast pumps and nursing supplies are exempt (since September 1, 2023), which is not taken out here.
Barber and beauty services, and auto repair labor: not taxed (FTA 2017 survey answer).
Clothing: maternity clothing is exempt (since September 1, 2023), which is not taken out here.
Laundry, dry cleaning and garment services are taxed, but coin-operated machines the customer runs are not.
Motor fuel is exempt from sales tax; the 20-cent-a-gallon state tax, left out here, has not been suspended (the September 28, 2026 disaster declaration eased diesel rules only, as reported).
Motor vehicle repair labor is not taxable; repair labor on other tangible property is (FTA 2017).

Hotel stays pay the 6% state hotel occupancy tax instead of sales tax, plus city, county and venue hotel taxes (Houston 17% in all; city taxes of 9% in Dallas and San Antonio, plus 2% for Bexar County, and 11% in Austin), which are not counted here (Comptroller; city pages). No local restaurant taxes were found beyond the sales tax.
Tobacco is assumed taxed at the general rate (excise taxes left out); not verified state by state.
gaps: Texas rates are from the Comptroller's city rates file (October 2026), which gives the total rate for each city in each county, with the special purpose districts and transit authorities that overlap it, and for named unincorporated communities. Each county part of a city takes the city's rate in that county; where parts of it (special purpose districts, transit areas) carry more, the highest is the top of the range shown for lost revenue. Named unincorporated communities are matched to the Census-designated place of the same name in the same county.

Unincorporated areas outside a named community take the county rate; special purpose districts and transit authorities (Houston METRO in unincorporated Harris County, VIA in unincorporated Bexar County, the Corpus Christi RTA in unincorporated Nueces County, Capital Metro in parts of Travis and Williamson counties) can add up to 2% local in all (8.25% total), the top of the range shown.

One row in the Comptroller's file looks wrong: unincorporated Williamson County within Williamson County ESD 2-A lists Capital Metro (Austin MTA) at 0%, for 7.25% in all, where the other 22 rows that list it give 1%. It changes no rate here: other rows already put Williamson County's unincorporated range at up to 2% local. The Comptroller has not been asked about it yet.

programs: Austin's Downtown and East 6th Street public improvement districts are mapped from the city's layer; its other districts aren't mapped (no city layer of them was found; their maps are PDFs). Its Financial Services department lists five active tax increment reinvestment zones (Mueller, Colony Park, Waller Creek, Dog's Head, approved July 2026, and the Brackenridge Tract); three business districts, the Downtown, East 6th Street and South Congress public improvement districts; a tourism district on hotels with more than 100 rooms (since January 2025); and three that pay for infrastructure in new developments (Whisper Valley, Estancia and Indian Hills).

Dallas' public improvement districts are the ones on the city's list of 15 active districts (October 2026), with boundaries as mapped in 2021. Not shown: the Tourism PID (hotels with 100 or more rooms anywhere in the city, through September 2029); Far East Dallas and Red Bird, which aren't in the city's layer (it publishes them only on a PDF map); and Prestonwood, a security district for about 1,000 homes rather than a business district. Midtown is shown under the boundary of the Vickery Meadow PID, its former name.

Fort Worth's business districts are shown (Downtown, Stockyards, Sun Valley, Historic Camp Bowie and East Lancaster Avenue). Of the city's other public improvement districts, the Tourism PID (18) and Panther Island (23) aren't in its map layer, and Park Glen, Heritage, Chapel Hill, Trinity Bluff, Walsh Ranch/Quail Valley, Rock Creek Ranch, Las Vegas Trail and Veale Ranch pay for upkeep in neighborhoods and new developments rather than business districts, so they aren't shown.
